title: "Run It Top to Bottom"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Why Notebooks Diff Badly (helpful, not required), Python 3 and the two exercise files below (about 1 KB).
**Objective:** show that a notebook's stored result can differ from a fresh top-to-bottom run, and use that as the check before you trust or share one.
**Time:** about 15 minutes.

<span class="ao-badge">Verified: ran run_cells.py on 2026-11-16 (macOS, Python 3.9.6). Output below is the real output. Tool facts: Last verified (docs, not run): marimo and Claude Code docs on 2026-11-16.</span>

**Files:** [cells.py](../../exercises/scriptorium/cells.py) and [run_cells.py](../../exercises/scriptorium/run_cells.py). Save both into an empty folder.
:::

## Hidden state

A notebook kernel (the background process that runs the cells' code) keeps variables in memory. You can run cells in any order, run one twice, or delete one after it ran. The variables stay. The page then shows a result that the file, read from the top, does not produce. This is hidden state, and it needs no agent to appear.

`cells.py` is a mock notebook with four cells, written in a `py:percent`-like style (the `# %% [1] load` headers carry our own numbers, so this is not standard `py:percent`). `run_cells.py` runs cells in the order you give, sharing one namespace like a kernel. It uses `exec`, so do not point it at files you did not write. First, the session an author might have had: cells 1 to 4, then cell 3 again to see the effect of the stricter cutoff in cell 4.

```bash
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4 3
```

```
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 2
```

The last screen shows `reads kept: 2`. Now run it the way a colleague would, top to bottom, in a fresh process:

```bash
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4
```

```
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
```

The file says 3 and the author's screen said 2. Cell 4 changes the cutoff after the cell that uses it, so the file as written never produces the 2.

## The habit

Before you trust or share a notebook, restart the kernel and run all cells from the top ("Restart Kernel and Run All" in Jupyter). If the result changes, the stored output was not a product of the file as written. A fresh run rules out hidden state; it does not show the analysis is right. Then fix the order so that cells only depend on cells above them.

Two related options:

- **Run it headless** (non-interactive, no one at the screen). *General practice:* on a cluster, run notebooks as a batch job, not as an interactive Jupyter session on the login node. Your cluster's policy decides (see the Citadel quests).
- **marimo.** Its docs describe a reactive model: deleting a cell scrubs its variables from memory, which the docs say eliminates hidden state, and a notebook can be run as a script with `python your_notebook.py`. Check the docs for how side effects (files, network) behave, because this quest did not test that.

*General practice:* pin the environment too (a container or lockfile), so a fresh run happens with the same packages, and do not let an agent `pip install` into a shared environment.

## Reviewing a notebook an agent edited

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

`NotebookEdit` changes one cell at a time. When it replaces a code cell, that cell's execution count and saved outputs are cleared. To get outputs back, re-run the cell and the cells that depend on it. So a notebook an agent touched shows either empty outputs or old outputs from cells it did not touch, which no longer match the new code. Re-run top to bottom yourself.

Then check the numbers with something the agent did not write, as in the Ground Truth quest in the Maze: compute one or two values independently and compare. A fresh run that completes is not proof that the analysis is right.

## OpenCode + Ollama

The habit does not depend on the tool: restart, run all, and check a few numbers independently. This quest makes no claims about how OpenCode edits notebooks; check its docs.

:::

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [marimo documentation](https://docs.marimo.io/): marimo, docs. Why read: it describes reactive cells that re-run in dependency order, a notebook design where hidden run-order state is harder to create.
- [The Notebook file format](https://nbformat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format_description.html): nbformat, docs. Why read: it is the spec showing that a notebook stores outputs and execution counts in its JSON, which is where a stale stored result lives.
:::
